opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that we're nowhere near the limits yet, and the reason is that the consumer of search has changed. For twenty-five years, search was optimized for a human looking at ten blue links. The human does a lot of the work: they skim, they click, they reformulate the query, they judge which sources to trust. So "quality" was really about ranking well enough that a person could finish the job.

When the consumer is an AI agent, the bar moves. The agent can read far more than a person ever would, but it's also less forgiving in some ways. It needs the right tokens, not just the right page. It needs evidence it can cite, freshness it can rely on, and some signal of how confident it should be. So the question becomes: how much compute and how much intelligence do you put behind a single query? Once you allow a search to take seconds or minutes instead of milliseconds, and to cost more, the quality ceiling goes way up. You can go deeper into the web, cross-reference sources, and verify claims.

So the limits I think about are less about the algorithms and more about three things. First, the open web itself: how much high-quality information is accessible, and whether the incentives exist for people to keep creating and publishing it. Second, the cost-latency tradeoff: every quality gain has a price, and different tasks justify different points on that curve. Third, evaluation: it's hard to improve what you can't measure, and measuring whether an agent got the genuinely correct, complete answer to a hard research question is much harder than measuring clicks.

My bet is that the web will increasingly be used by AIs more than by humans, and that justifies rebuilding a lot of the stack, from crawling and indexing to how we rank and package results, with that new user in mind. We're early on that curve, and there's a lot of quality left to unlock.

r001.rationale: The response says search quality is far from its limits, but it does not identify billion-to-billion matching as the open-ended problem.

r002.rationale: It describes a cost-latency tradeoff and says quality gains have a price, with different tasks justifying different points on that curve.

r003.rationale: It discusses compute and intelligence, but does not suggest that AI intelligence is becoming cheaper or that this keeps improvements economically worthwhile.

r004.rationale: The response advocates rebuilding the search stack, but does not say that even a small quality advantage creates a competitive edge.

fable-5.1.text:
So the honest answer is that I don't think there's a hard ceiling that we're anywhere close to, but the shape of the problem changes as you go up the quality curve.

At the low end, quality is mostly about retrieval. Can you find the right documents, do you have fresh enough coverage of the web, do you have an index that's actually good? That's a well-understood engineering problem. It's expensive, but you know how to make progress on it. A lot of what we've been building at Parallel is in that layer, because when we started, most people were putting a beautiful model on top of a pretty mediocre retrieval stack, and the model was doing a lot of work to compensate.

Once retrieval is good, the limits move somewhere more interesting. The question becomes: what does the task actually require? If someone asks for a quick fact, the ceiling is basically there already. If someone asks for a deep research answer that needs forty sources reconciled against each other, then quality is bounded by how much compute you're willing to spend, how good the model is at reasoning over conflicting evidence, and whether you can verify the answer rather than just produce it. Those are all still improving, and I don't see a wall.

The thing I'd push on is that "quality" in isolation isn't the right frame. It's quality at a given cost and latency. You can almost always get a better answer by spending more, running more searches, doing more verification passes. The real limit is the trade-off curve, and the whole game is pushing that frontier out. What was expensive and slow last year becomes cheap and fast this year, and that opens up tasks that weren't worth doing before.

The other limit, which people underrate, is the web itself. Some things aren't written down anywhere, or they're written down wrong, or the source is paywalled or behind a login. No amount of model intelligence fixes that. So part of thinking about limits is being honest about when the answer is "the information doesn't exist in a form I can reach," and saying that, instead of hallucinating something plausible. I'd actually rather have a system that knows its limits than one that's slightly better on average but confidently wrong at the tail.

r001.rationale: The response says search quality has no nearby hard ceiling, but it does not identify billion-to-billion matching as the open-ended problem.

r002.rationale: It describes a quality, cost, and latency trade-off, but does not say improvement should stop when incremental gains cease to justify their cost.

r003.rationale: It says that what was expensive and slow can become cheap and fast, making previously uneconomical tasks worthwhile and allowing the frontier to keep moving.

r004.rationale: The response does not claim that an incremental quality advantage creates a competitive edge.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two different limits. One is whether the information exists and is accessible on the web. The other is whether the system can find it, understand it, and use it to answer your question. Better models can help a lot with the second problem, but they don’t automatically solve the first.

And then there’s the question of what you mean by quality. If you ask a simple factual question, you can often tell whether the answer is correct. But if you’re researching a decision, quality depends on whether the system understands what matters to you, finds the relevant perspectives, and distinguishes strong evidence from something that merely sounds convincing.

So I don’t think we’re close to exhausting the improvements available. But the goal can’t just be to produce a more fluent answer. It has to be to give you a better-supported answer—and to recognize when the available information doesn’t justify a confident one.

r001.rationale: The response says search quality improvements are not exhausted, but it does not present billion-to-billion matching as the open-ended problem.

r002.rationale: It does not frame the practical limit as whether incremental gains justify their cost.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that cheaper AI intelligence could keep improvements economically worthwhile.

r004.rationale: It does not argue that even a small quality advantage could create a competitive edge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: what’s limiting quality today? Sometimes the information is on the web, but you haven’t found it. Sometimes you’ve found the right sources, but the model hasn’t understood them or combined them correctly. And sometimes the information simply isn’t there, or the sources disagree. Those are very different problems.

For the first two, I think there’s substantial room to improve—better retrieval, better reasoning, and a tighter loop between the two. The model can recognize that it’s missing something and go look for it. But you eventually run into the limits of the available evidence. At that point, improving quality means being clear about what you know, what you don’t know, and how confident the user should be in the answer.
